titleEn: Laws of Hammurabi — §127–140: slander, marriage, adultery and divorce (xxi 25 – xxiii 32)
part: Laws §127–140 · slander, marriage, adultery & divorce (Col. xxi 25 – xxiii 32)
about: Fourteen laws on the family. The first punishes a man who accuses a woman of misconduct and cannot prove it (§127): he is thrown down before the judges and half (of his hair) is shaved. A marriage whose contracts have not been set is no marriage (§128). Then the adultery laws: a wife caught with another man is bound and thrown into the water with him, unless her husband spares her and the king spares his servant (§129); a man who holds down a man’s wife who has not known a male and lives in her father’s house is killed, and the woman is released (§130). A wife merely accused by her husband swears the oath of the god and goes home (§131); one only spoken against must plunge into the River for her husband’s sake (§132). Next the captivity laws: a wife whose husband has been carried off may stay in her house, and if there is food she must (§133, partly restored), if she goes elsewhere she is thrown into the water (§133A), but if there is no food she bears no blame (§134); if she has borne children in the other house, she goes back to her first husband when he returns, and the sons follow their own father (§135); a man who abandons his city loses his wife (§136). The last laws are on divorce: a man who divorces a wife who has borne him children gives her back her dowry and half the field, orchard and goods, and she raises the children, takes a share like one heir’s, and marries whom she likes (§137); one who divorces a childless wife gives her her bride-price and dowry (§138); and where there was no bride-price, a mina of silver, or a third of a mina if he is a commoner (§139–140). Harper’s transliteration is followed. Lines XXII 12–17 are broken and printed in brackets: they are Harper’s restorations, not stone. Several words are uncertain and are said so in the notes: ugbabtum, šugītum, the restored pagarša, the verbs urabbâ and urtabbû, uzubbûm and ḫāwirum.

sentences.l: If a-man against an-ugbabtum (?) and the-wife of-a-man the-finger he-made-point-and, not he-proved,
sentences.i: If a man has had a finger pointed at an ugbabtum (a priestess?) or at another man’s wife, and has not proved it,
sentences.n: The slander laws begin, and the first is one long “if”. Read it clause by clause: eli “against, at”, then two women, then the verb. ubānam ušatrīṣma is “he made a finger point”, the code’s idiom for an accusation: ubānum “finger”, ušatrīṣ the Š-stem of tarāṣum “to stretch out, point” (the t is part of the root), with -ma “and”. lā uktīn is “he did not prove (it)”, the D-stem of kânum, the same verb as ukannūšuma in §112. aššat is aššatum “wife” in the construct state, “the wife of” a man. The conjunction u is written ù. The sign group read ugbabtum is UNCERTAIN: Harper prints NIN.AN here and gives it no reading, and the plate agrees with his print. After e-li it shows the hexagon sign with the small boxed-wedge sign that together spell NIN, and then AN; the second hexagon with its long tail, which stands in front of them at XVIII 36 (§110, where the group is ŠAL.NIN.AN), is not there, so no ŠAL is written. It is read ugbabtum, a priestess, as in §110, which is no more certain. The code never reads it nadītum.

sentences.l: that man before the-judges they-shall-throw-him-down, and his-half they-shall-shave.
sentences.i: they shall throw that man down before the judges and shave half (of his hair).
sentences.n: The apodosis. Both verbs are plural with no subject written: “they” means the court. inaddûšu is nadûm “to throw, cast down” with -šu “him” (nadûm, not nadānum “to give”: the weak ending -û shows it). maḫar dajjānī is “before the judges”. muttassu is Harper’s mu-ut-ta-zu: muttatum is “half” (it returns in §137 as muttat eqlim, “half of the field”) and -zu is -šu after the t, said -ssu, so “his half”; the hair is understood, not written. ugallabū is the D-stem of galābum “to shave”, plural, “they shall shave”. The penalty is shame in public, not death.

sentences.l: If a-man a-wife he-took-and, her-contracts not he-set, woman that not a-wife.
sentences.i: If a man has taken a wife and has not set down her contracts, that woman is not a wife.
sentences.n: A short law with a two-part “if” and a flat verdict with no verb at all: zinništum šī ul aššat is “that woman — not (a) wife”, a nominal sentence, “is” understood. iḫuzma is aḫāzum “to take” (here “to take in marriage”) in the preterite, with -ma (iḫuz; the perfect would have the -ta- after the first sign); iškun is šakānum “to set, place”, so lā iškun is “he did not set down”. riksātiša is “her bonds”, the contracts that make a marriage binding; the same noun, riksātum, is “contracts” in the earlier laws. zinništum “woman” is written with the single sign SAL (Harper’s zinništum for the plate’s one sign), the same sign that spells aššatum “wife” in §26–41 and again at XXII 75 (aššatim): only the context says “woman” or “wife”. šī is “she, that”, the feminine of šū.

sentences.l: If the-wife of-a-man with a-male another in lying was-seized, they-shall-bind-them-and into the-water they-shall-throw-them,
sentences.i: If a man’s wife is caught lying with another male, they shall bind them and throw them into the water.
sentences.n: Adultery, and the verdict is drowning, stated plainly. zikārum is “male”, šanûm “other, second”; ina itūlim is “in lying (together)”. Harper prints i-tu-lim here but u-tu-lim at XXI 72 (§131); both are as printed. ittaṣbat is the N-stem perfect of ṣabātum “to seize”, a passive: “was seized, caught” (the N-stem passive). ikassûšunūtima: the verb is probably kasûm “to bind” (Harper’s i-ka-zu spells it with the ZU sign, read su here; the verb is not certain), then -šunūti “them” and -ma, so “they shall bind them and”. inaddûšunūti is the same verb as inaddûšu in §127, nadûm “to throw”, now with “them”: “they shall throw them”. ana mê is “into the water”; mû, “water”, has the plural form mê. The two are thrown in together, the wife and her partner.

sentences.l: If the-owner of-the-wife his-wife he-lets-live, and the-king his-servant he-lets-live.
sentences.i: If the wife’s husband lets his wife live, then the king shall let his servant live too.
sentences.n: A second “if” inside the same law, a pardon: bēl aššatim “the owner of the wife” is her husband. aššassu is aššat + -šu, “his wife”, spelled aš-ša-zu (the -šu becomes -zu, said -ssu, after the t); in the same way wara-zu is warad + -šu, said warassu, “his servant”, written with the single sign ARAD and zu. The verb is balāṭum “to live”, in the D-stem uballaṭ “he makes live, spares”: the first is the husband’s act, the second the king’s. The servant is understood to be the other man, the wife’s partner, whom only the king may spare; the text says only “his servant”. wara-zu is Harper’s print for ARAD-zu, the logogram ARAD “servant, slave” with zu.

sentences.l: If a-man the-wife of-a-man who a-male not she-knew-and in the-house of-her-father is-living, he-held-her-down-and,
sentences.i: If a man has held down a man’s wife — one who has not known a male and is living in her father’s house —
sentences.n: A law about force, and the text states it without softening. ša zikaram lā īdûma is “who (has) not known a male”: edûm “to know”, subjunctive -u after ša, then -ma. ina bīt abiša wašbat “in her father’s house she dwells”: wašbat is the stative of wašābum, “she is living”; bīt, “house of”, is the construct of É. ukabbilšima is Harper’s u-kab-bil-ši-ma: the verb is kabālum in the D-stem, “to bind, hold fast”, with -ši “her” and -ma. “Held her down” is the sense taken here, not certain. The sign read kab is no. 46 of Harper’s List of Signs (kab), and the plate shows a sign of that shape in that place (XXI 60). The text calls her “a man’s wife” and says she is still living in her father’s house; it says no more about her situation. The law runs on into the next unit.

sentences.l: in her-lap he-lay-and they-seized-him, that man he-shall-be-killed, that woman she-shall-be-released.
sentences.i: and has lain in her lap, and they have caught him, that man shall be killed; that woman shall be released.
sentences.n: The rest of the protasis, then the verdict. ina sūniša is “in her lap, her bosom”; Harper’s zu-ni-ša has the sign ZU, read su, so sūnum (the form is not certain). ittatīlma is a perfect of the verb of itūlum “to lie (with)”, with -ma; the same stem gives itūlum in §129. iṣṣabtūšu is ṣabātum “to seize”, the perfect plural (the t of the perfect is taken into the ṣ, as in iṣṣabat), “they seized him”: caught in the act. awīlum šū iddâk “that man shall be killed” (the house rendering of iddâk); zinništum šī ūtaššar is “that woman shall be released”, ūtaššar being the Dt-stem of wašārum, “to be released”, as in the sealed-receipt laws (§100–111). The man dies and the woman is cleared: she is the victim. The two verdicts are set side by side, awīlum šū and zinništum šī, “that man” and “that woman”.

sentences.l: If the-wife of-a-man her-husband accused-her-and, with a-male another in lying not she-was-seized,
sentences.i: If a man’s wife has been accused by her husband, but has not been caught lying with another male,
sentences.n: Harper prints aš-sa-at, with a plain s, on XXI 68; as printed. mussa is mut + -ša, “her husband” (mutum “husband”, with a short u: mūtum “death” is another word; written mu-za, the -ša becoming -za after the dental). ubbiršima is the D-stem of abārum (ubburum), “to accuse, charge”, with -ši “her” and -ma: the verb of ubbirma in §1, not the bârum of §126 (ubâr, “to prove”). utūlim is Harper’s u-tu-lim, the same word as itūlim in §129; as printed. lā iṣṣabit is “she was not seized”: iṣṣabit is the N-stem preterite of ṣabātum (inṣabit, the n taken into the ṣ), a passive, as ittaṣbat, the N perfect, was in §129 and §132. This is the wife who is charged by her own husband but has not been caught with anyone.

sentences.l: the-oath of-the-god she-shall-swear-and to her-house she-shall-return.
sentences.i: she shall swear the oath of the god and go back to her house.
sentences.n: The verdict is an oath, not a punishment. nīš ilim izakkar, “she shall swear the oath of the god” (the house rendering, as in the merchant laws); izakkarma is zakārum, the present with -ma. The oath clears her, and ana bītiša itâr “to her house she shall return” sends her back home. bīti-ša is written É-ti-ša: É, the house-sign, with ti and ša. itâr is târum “to return” in the present, the usual “shall return”.

sentences.l: If the-wife of-a-man because-of a-male another the-finger against-her was-pointed-and, with a-male another in lying not she-was-seized,
sentences.i: If a finger has been pointed at a man’s wife because of another male, and she has not been caught lying with another male,
sentences.n: The same idea as §127, seen from the wife’s side: ubānum eliša ittariṣma is “a finger was pointed against her”, with ittariṣ the N-stem preterite (a passive) of tarāṣum (where §127 had the Š-stem, “he made point”); the N-stem of tarāṣum is read from the form and the sense (UNCERTAIN as a form). aššum, “because of, on account of”, takes zikārim šanîm, “another male”. eliša is eli + -ša, “against her”. The last verb is again the N-stem of ṣabātum, now the perfect, spelled it-ta-aṣ-ba-at (§129 has it-ta-aṣ-bat). The unit crosses into column XXII at line 1. A law of rumour: no witness, no deed, only talk. The next unit gives the remedy.

sentences.l: for her-husband the-divine-River she-shall-plunge.
sentences.i: for her husband’s sake she shall plunge into the River.
sentences.n: This is the river ordeal, as in §2: the verdict is left to the water. The sign group {d}ÍD (the divine-name marker, the river-sign A with ENGUR) is the River as a god: Harper reads it Nâru, here in the accusative, Nāram, with the god’s determinative silent in the readable form. išalli is the present of šalûm, “to sink, plunge”: she goes into the river and the god decides. ana mutiša is “for her husband (’s sake)”, mutiša being mutim + -ša (mutum “husband”, as in §131). Oath for the charged wife, River for the talked-about one: the River decides what no witness has seen.

sentences.l: If a-man he-was-carried-off-and, in his-house of eating there-is,
sentences.i: If a man has been carried off, and there is food in his house,
sentences.n: The captivity laws (§133–136). iššalilma is the N-stem preterite of šalālum “to carry off, take as booty”: “was carried off” (here, taken away as a captive), a passive, with -ma. ša akālim ibašši is “there is (something) of eating”, that is food: ša, “of”, with the infinitive akālim “eating”, and ibašši “there is”, from bašûm. bīti-šu is “his house”, written É-ti-šu. The words are Harper’s transliteration, as printed. The first line is the plain “if” of a law, and the law goes on in the next unit, which Harper shows in brackets.

sentences.l: [his-wife in her-house she-stays, her-body (?) she-shall-guard, to a-house another not she-shall-enter.]
sentences.i: [his wife shall stay in her own house, guard her person (?), and not go into another house.]
sentences.n: All of this unit is Harper’s restoration: on the plate XXII 13–15 are hatched (the stone is damaged there and only the last sign or two of each line survive), and on 12 and 16–18 Harper draws his restored signs in outline; he prints the words in square brackets, even cutting into words ([i-na bî]-za, [pa-gar-š]a, [wa-az-za-a]t). They are not on the stone and are not reconstructed any further. The sense follows from the next laws (§133A, 134), which repeat the same words: aššassu, “his wife”, wazzat, the stative of uzuzzum “to stand, stay”, pagarša, from pagrum “body” (Harper’s restoration; Kohler–Ungnad restore “her property”, NÍG.GA-ša, in the same place, so “her person” is a guess and UNCERTAIN), inaṣṣar, “she shall guard”, naṣārum, and ana bītim šanîm ul irrub, “into another house she shall not enter”. bīssa is bīt + -ša, spelled É-za. The ending of wa-az-za-a]t is broken: the last sign is at.

sentences.l: [If] woman that her-body (?) not she-guarded-and, to a-house another she-entered,
sentences.i: If that woman has not guarded her person (?) but has gone into another house,
sentences.n: Harper’s headings call this stretch §133A; here it is carried under §133 with no number of its own, so the law numbers run 127–140. It is the rule for the wife who does not keep to her house: the first words are bracketed (š[um-ma], [pa]-gar-ša), restored by Harper. iṣṣurma is naṣārum “to guard” in the preterite (the n of the root is taken into the ṣ: inṣur becomes iṣṣur), written iṣ-ṣur-ma, with -ma; lā iṣṣurma is “she did not guard”. The sign read ṣur is no. 167 of Harper’s List of Signs, and the plate shows a sign of that shape in that place (XXII 20). pagarša is “her body, her person”: restored by Harper (the Susa duplicates are broken here; Kohler–Ungnad restore “her property” instead), UNCERTAIN. īterub is erēbum “to enter” in the perfect: the perfect has the -ta- after the first sign, here te in i-te-ru-ub. The perfect, “has entered”, is the tense of the fact done; the present, irrub, is used for “enters, goes in” in the laws that follow.

sentences.l: woman that they-shall-convict-her-and, into the-water they-shall-throw-her.
sentences.i: they shall convict that woman and throw her into the water.
sentences.n: The penalty is the same drowning as in §129, said in the same words. zinništam šuāti is “that woman” in the accusative (the -m ending of the object). ukannūšima is kânum in the D-stem, “to convict, prove against”, plural with -ši “her” and -ma: the same verb as uktīn in §127 and ukannūšuma in §112, so “they shall convict her”. ana mê inaddûši is “they shall throw her into the water”, nadûm with -ši “her”. The sign group before the verb is the one SAL sign, as for every “woman” in this part. The law gives no reason; none is read into it.

sentences.l: If a-man he-was-carried-off-and, in his-house of-eating not there-is,
sentences.i: If a man has been carried off and there is no food in his house,
sentences.n: The mirror of §133: the same “if” with one new word. lā ibašši is “there is not”, the negative lā before the present of bašûm; ša akālim is again “of eating”, “food” (Harper’s ša a-ka-li-im, so akālim). Everything in the first line is as in §133. Unlike §133, this law carries no brackets in Harper’s transliteration; it is read from his print line by line. A man in captivity leaves no food in the house; the next unit says what the wife may then do.

sentences.l: his-wife to a-house another she-enters, woman that blame not she-has.
sentences.i: and his wife goes into another house, that woman bears no blame.
sentences.n: The verdict is the opposite of §133A: ar-nam ul īšu is “blame she does not have” (arnum, “guilt, blame, fault”; īšu, “she has”, from išûm “to have”, with the ul before it). Note that irrub, “she enters”, is the present and not a command or a permission: it says what happens and then what follows. aššassu, “his wife”, is as in §129. The rule says only that there is no guilt for going into another house when there is no food in his house. §135 follows with the case of the husband’s return.

sentences.l: If a-man he-was-carried-off-and, in his-house of-eating not there-is, before him his-wife to a-house another she-entered-and,
sentences.i: If a man has been carried off and there is no food in his house, and, before his return (?), his wife has gone into another house,
sentences.n: A long “if”, built from §134 with a new clause. ana pānīšu is literally “before him, to his face”; the sense taken here is “before his return”, UNCERTAIN as to the exact force (“before him” itself says nothing about a return). pānum is “face, front”. īterubma is erēbum “to enter” in the perfect with -ma (cf. the plain īterub in §133A). The unit ends on that -ma: the sentence goes on with the children and the husband’s return. Everything else is as in §134. Notice the pattern of the whole captivity block: a conditional with one condition per law, each ending in a verdict about the wife.

sentences.l: children she-bore, afterwards her-husband he-returned-and his-city he-reached,
sentences.i: and she has borne children, and afterwards her husband has come back and reached his city,
sentences.n: In the scan the last vowel of mârê (here mārī, “children, sons”) on XXII 46 is partly blotted; it is read by analogy with XXII 54. It is written DUMU with the plural sign (the readable form drops it): DUMU{meš}. ittalad is walādum “to bear (children)” in the perfect, “she has borne”. ina warka is “afterwards”, warka, “behind, afterwards”. mussa (mu-za) is “her husband”, as in §131. ittūramma is târum “to return” in the perfect with the ventive -am, “he came back” (the ventive means “back to here”), with -ma. ālšu iktašdam is “his city he reached”: iktašdam is kašādum, “to reach, arrive at”, in the perfect with the ventive. ali-šu is written with the city-sign URU and šu.

sentences.l: woman that to her-husband she-shall-return, the-sons after their-father they-shall-go.
sentences.i: that woman shall go back to her husband; the sons shall follow their father.
sentences.n: In the scan the i of ši-i on XXII 51 looks slightly malformed (the dot faint); read ši-i. ana ḫāwiriša is “to her husband”: ḫāwirum is a word for “husband, spouse” (Harper’s “husband”), here with -ša; it is a rarer word than mutum, and “first husband” is the sense the situation suggests (the husband she had before), not a certainty. itâr is târum, “she shall return”. mārū warki abišunu illakū is “the sons after their father shall go”: mārū, the nominative plural of mārum, spelled with the same DUMU sign; warki, “after, behind”; abišunu is “their father” (abum with -šunu); illakū, “they shall go”, from alākum. The children stay with their father’s line, whatever the wife’s second marriage.

sentences.l: If a-man his-city he-abandoned-and he-fled, after-him his-wife to a-house another she-entered,
sentences.i: If a man has abandoned his city and run away, and his wife, behind him, has entered another house,
sentences.n: A man who leaves of his own will, not one who is taken. ālšu iddīma is “he threw off his city, abandoned it”: nadûm “to throw, leave” in the preterite with -ma (cf. iddīma in §1). ittabit is “he fled”, the verb nabātum “to flee, run away” in the perfect (Harper’s nabâṭu; the verb is not certain). warkišu is warki + -šu, “after him”. The rest is as in §135: the wife goes into another house. The law runs on over the next two units.

sentences.l: If a-man that he-returned-and his-wife he-has-seized,
sentences.i: and if that man has come back and has taken hold of his wife,
sentences.n: A second “if” inside the same law: šumma awīlum šū is “if that man” (šū, “that, he”). ittūramma is târum “to return” in the perfect with the ventive (-am) and -ma, as in §135. iṣṣabat is ṣabātum “to seize, take hold of”, here in the sense of reclaiming his wife (the perfect: the t of the perfect is taken into the ṣ, iṣbat + -ta- giving iṣṣabat; it is the tense of the act done). The sentence is not finished: the verdict comes in the next unit, and it begins with the reason, aššum, “because”. Read the three units as one law: the husband flees, the wife remarries, the husband returns.

sentences.l: because his-city he-hated-and he-fled, the-wife of-a-fugitive to her-husband not she-shall-return.
sentences.i: because he hated his city and fled, the wife of a runaway shall not go back to her husband.
sentences.n: The verdict gives its reason first. aššum, “because”, takes the subjunctive: izīrūma is zêrum “to hate, loathe”, with -u and -ma (izīru + ma), and innabitu is the N-stem of nabātum “to flee”, also with -u (the subjunctive ending, here after aššum), “because he hated his city and fled”. The N-stem is UNCERTAIN: Harper writes in-na-bi-tu. aššat munnabtim is “the wife of a fugitive”, aššat in the construct state, munnabtim, “of a runaway” (Harper’s mu-na-ab-tim, with one n). ana mutiša ul itâr, “to her husband she shall not return”: the man who runs from his city loses his wife.

sentences.l: If a-man to a-šugītum who children she-bore-to-him, or a-wife who children she-caused-him-to-have, to-divorce his-face he-set,
sentences.i: If a man has set his face to divorce a šugītum who has borne him children, or a wife who has provided him with children,
sentences.n: The divorce laws begin. šugītum is written with ŠAL (the woman-sign, a determinative here) before šu-gi₄-tim (Harper prints šu-ge-tim): Harper’s ge is his sign no. 122 (gi, GE), the sign the plate shows here (XXII 74), the same as the GE of MAL.GE.A in §110: a class of woman named only here, whom the law sets beside an ordinary wife as one who may bear children; her exact status is UNCERTAIN. ša mārī ūlidušum is “who (has) borne children to him” (walādum, subjunctive -u before -šum “to him”, so ūlidušum); ulu is “or” (the two kinds of woman); ušaršušu is the Š-stem of rašûm “to have, acquire”, ušarši + the subjunctive -u + -šu “him”, “who has made him acquire (children)”, the same sense in other words; the analysis of the ending is UNCERTAIN. The idiom is ezēbim pānīšu ištakan, “he has set his face to divorce”: ezēbum “to leave, divorce” (Harper’s e-ṣi-bi-im spells the ZI sign as ṣi, said zi), pānum “face”, and šakānum “to set”. Harper prints one a-na only, before the woman; ezēbim has none of its own.

sentences.l: to woman that her-dowry they-shall-return-to-her, and half of-the-field, orchard and goods they-shall-give-her-and,
sentences.i: they shall give that woman back her dowry, and give her half of the field, the orchard and the goods,
sentences.n: The wife’s portion. šeriqtaša is her šeriqtum, the dowry (the gift from her father’s house): Harper reads the word with q (še-ri-iq-ta-ša, the sign IG read iq), and modern editions read it with k. utarrūšim is târum “to return” in the D-stem, “to give back”, plural, with -šim “to her”. muttat eqlim kirêm u bīšim is “half of field, orchard and goods”: muttatum “half”, then three nouns joined by u. The field is A.ŠÀ-lim, the orchard {giš}KIRI₆ (Harper’s kirêm, said kirîm after the genitive; the sign read as the orchard-sign), the goods bīšim, “property”. inaddinūšimma is nadānum “to give” in the present, plural, with -šim “to her” and -ma. The unit runs over into column XXIII at line 1.

sentences.l: her-children she-shall-bring-up; after her-children she-has-brought-up,
sentences.i: she shall bring up her children. After she has brought up her children,
sentences.n: mārī-ša is “her children”, written DUMU, with the plural sign, and ša. The two verbs are the D-stem of rabûm “to grow”, “to bring up”: urabbâ (u-ra-ab-ba) “she shall bring up”, and urtabbû (ur-ta-ab-bu-u) “she has brought up”, the D perfect with the subjunctive -u after ištu, so the children are the object both times. Both forms are UNCERTAIN: the ending of the first is not clear, and the second could be read differently (the sense, that she raises them and that the next step comes when they are grown, is clear). ištu is “after, since”. Because inaddinūšimma at the end of the unit before ends in -ma, this continues the same sentence: a wife who has been divorced keeps the children and brings them up; only then is her own future settled.

sentences.l: from whatever that to her-children was-given, a-portion like an-heir one they-shall-give-her-and,
sentences.i: from everything that was given to her children they shall give her a share equal to one heir’s,
sentences.n: ina mimma ša … innadnu is “from whatever was given”: ina, “from, out of”, mimma “whatever”, ša with the subjunctive innadnu, the N-stem passive of nadānum, “was given”; ana mārīša is “to her children”. zittam is “a share, portion” (zittum; Harper’s ṣi-it-tam, the ZI sign read ṣi by Harper and zi here, as in ezēbim), kīma aplim ištēn is “like one heir”: aplum, “heir, son”, ištēn “one”. inaddinūšimma is as in the previous unit. The point is that the divorced wife, once her children are brought up, takes from what was given to her children a share like that of a single heir, not more.

sentences.l: the-husband of her-heart he-shall-take-her.
sentences.i: and the husband of her heart (the man she likes) shall take her as wife.
sentences.n: mut libbiša is “the husband of her heart”, the man she herself chooses (mutum “husband”, then libbum “heart, mind”, with -ša “her”). iḫḫazzi is aḫāzum “to take” in the present with -ši “her”, the š becoming z after the z of the stem: iḫḫaz-ši is said iḫḫazzi, “he shall take her (as wife)”. So the woman’s next marriage is her own decision. The verbs change subject: “they” (not named) give her the share, “he”, the new husband, takes her.

sentences.l: If a-man his-wife who children not she-bore-to-him he-divorces,
sentences.i: If a man divorces his wife who has not borne him children,
sentences.n: ḫīrtašu is “his wife”: ḫīrtum, “wife” (Harper), with -šu. ša mārī lā ūlidušum is “who has not borne him children”: the relative ša, mārī “children”, lā, and the verb as in §137 with the subjunctive -u before -šum “to him”. izzib is the present of ezēbum “to leave, divorce” (the preterite is īzib), spelled i-iz-zi-ib: “he divorces”. The verdict comes in the next two units.

sentences.l: silver as-much-as her-bride-price he-shall-give-her, and the-dowry
sentences.i: he shall give her silver to the amount of her bride-price, and also the dowry
sentences.n: kaspam mala tirḫatiša is “silver as much as her bride-price”: kaspam is written KÙ.BABBAR-am; mala “as much as”; tirḫatum is the bride-price, the marriage payment (understood as the groom’s gift) (Harper’s tir-ḫa-ti-ša; the sign read tir is no. 145 of Harper’s List of Signs, and the plate shows that shape at the start of XXIII 19). inaddiššim is nadānum “to give” in the present with -šim “to her”, spelled i-na-ad-di-iš-ši-im: inaddin + -šim, the n taken into the š, gives inaddiššim. ù šeriqtam is “and the dowry” (as in §137, with q). The sentence goes on into the next unit.

sentences.l: which from the-house of-her-father she-brought he-shall-make-good-to-her-and he-shall-divorce-her.
sentences.i: which she brought from her father’s house he shall make good to her, and then divorce her.
sentences.n: ša ištu bīt abiša ublam is “which from her father’s house she brought”: ša, then ištu “from”, bīt abiša “the house of her father”, and ublam, wabālum “to bring” (the ventive -am, “brought here”). ušallamšimma is šalāmum in the D-stem, “to make whole, make good”, with -šim “to her” and -ma: “he shall make it good to her”, meaning he gives her the whole dowry back. izzibši is ezēbum “to divorce” with -ši “her”, “he shall divorce her” (Harper’s i-iz-zi-ib-ši). Note that ublam has the ventive -am where a subjunctive -u would stand; after ša the ventive takes its place.

sentences.l: If bride-price not there-is, one mina of-silver for divorce-payment he-shall-give-her.
sentences.i: If there is no bride-price, he shall give her one mina of silver as a divorce payment.
sentences.n: A short law, with the sums fixed. tirḫatum lā ibašši is “bride-price there is not”: lā ibašši, as in §134. The amount is I MA.NA KÙ.BABBAR-im, which Harper writes I ma-na kaspim: I is the sign for one (the plate has one wedge), ma-na “mina”, kaspim “of silver”, so ištēn mana kaspim, “one mina of silver”. ana uzubbîm is “as a divorce payment”: uzubbûm is the sum paid at a divorce (a rarer word, taken here from the context; UNCERTAIN as to the exact meaning). inaddiššim is as in §138. One mina is about half a kilogram of silver, 60 shekels.

sentences.l: If a-commoner, a-third mina of-silver he-shall-give-her.
sentences.i: If he is a commoner, he shall give her one-third of a mina of silver.
sentences.n: The sum drops for a commoner. šumma muškēnum is “if (he is) a commoner”: muškēnum, written MAŠ.EN.KAK, the code’s second rank, with no verb, “is” understood, the sentence standing on its own like §128. The fraction is Harper’s ⅓ ma-na kaspim: ⅓ is the plate’s fraction-sign (the same sign as in §114 and §116, spoken šalšāt (?), reconstructed), mana “mina”, kaspim “of silver”; one third of a mina is twenty shekels. inaddiššim is as in §138–139. With this law the part ends.
